column14: Volunteer male participants aged between 18 and 58 engaged in bodybuilding, registered in gyms in TRNC.
column30: Bodybuilding
column82: As muscle dysmorphia increases, orthorexia nervosa increases in individuals engaged in bodybuilding sports in the TRNC.
column83: Since this study was conducted only on male bodybuilders, the findings cannot be generalized to Female bodybuilders.
column84:
It is essential to provide education on muscle dysmorphia, orthorexia nervosa, and the use of ergogenic nutritional supplements in Physical Education and Sports Schools, as well as in coach training programs. Additionally, training on athlete nutrition and sports psychology in these institutions would equip them with knowledge about both athlete motivations and the mental health disorders frequently seen in athletes. Given the rise of these mental health issues in gyms, sports psychologists should be present in these environments, and mental health assessments should be conducted alongside medical evaluations for new memberships.
Conducting similar studies across different sports and with female participants could contribute valuable new insights to the literature.

column5: Ahlich, E., Choquette, E.M., Rancourt, D.
column14: 18-49 years, recruited using convenience sampling from a large southeastern university's research, receiving research credit upon completion of the study, informed consent
column30: Mixed sport
column82: The current findings support body talk and fat talk as a potential risk factor for eating disorders among male. Muscle-focused body talk may not a risk factor for diagnostic eating disorder symptoms. Muscle talk among male is related less to muscle dissatisfaction and more to male socioalization processes. Athletic identity did non emerge as a significant moderator of the association between body talk and eating disorder symptoms.
column83: The study was limited to a single university campus in the southeastern United States, limiting generalizability of the findings. Few participants endorsed aesthetic or lean sports, potentially attenuating results.
column84:
Future work may benefit from using a more objective of body composition. 
Future work should explore such associations among male in a clinical sample, examining whether fat or muscle talk is associated with eating disorder and/or muscle dysmorphia symptom severity. 
Fat talk may be an important prevention target amon male, regardless of athletic identity.

column5: Anderson, C.M., Petrie, T.A., Neumann, C.S.
column13:
Time 1: begin of the fall season (September)
Time 2: end of the season (February)
column14: Student athletes from 26 universities located within all regions of the United States
column30: Gymnastics, swimming, and divers
column57: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
column82: Sport pressures and dietary restraint were highly stable over the course of a competitive season. Pressures gymnasts and swimmers/divers experienced regarding body weight, size, and appearance from their coaches and teammates predicted decreases in their body satisfaction over a 5-month period, this change occurred even though the athletes’ body mass index did not change significantly over that time.
column83: Included only NCAA Division I Female gymnasts and swimmers/divers, who also happened to primarily be Caucasien. The authors examined the variables over only a 5-month period, which represented one competitive collegiate season for these athletes. They examined the relationships among only sport pressures, body dissatisfaction and dietary restraint, additional research is needed to examine other variables such as general sociatail pressures, internalization, and negative affect. The validity of self-report measures of dietary restraint as predictors of actual reductions in food intake has been challenged. Self report measures of dietary restraint are risk factors in the prediction of disordered eating attitudes and behaviors, the measures are poor predictors of behaviorally observed, acute dietary restriction. BMI did not vary over the course of the 5-month season, we were not able to obtain more sensitive measures of body composition due to the study's design.
column84:
Health care personnel can help coaches and teammates become more aware of how, through their behaviors and comments, they create an environment that pressures athletes about their body, weight, and appearance. Sport health care professionals can target sport administrators and sport-governing bodies because they have the power to male policy changes that can improve the sport environment, maling it less toxic for athletes. Such entities, could make revealing uniforms less so, adjust judging criteria so there is less focus on aesthetic/appearance-based aspects of the performance, expand or raise weight classifications, and/or set up strict requirements regarding acceptable weight loss over specific periods of time. Preventive programming, sport health care profesionals can work directly with athletes to help them counter these sport pressures and reduce their likelihood of engaging in caloric restriction of feeling dissatisfied with their bodies. 
Future reseach should examine whether our findings are supported in other groups of Female athletes (e.g., different sports, different competitive levels, more diverse racial/ethnic groups), male athletes should also be studied and such research should include measures of drive for muscularity. Other longitudinal studies may want to examine eating disorders and other potential risk factors over a longer period of time, or a different period (e.g., from the end of the competitive season to the start of the next one).

column82: This study did not find significant correlations between criticism received on social media and disordered eating behaviors in college gymnasts. Combining variables related to social hassles, body satisfaction, usage of certain social media outlets, and years of participation could perdict disordered eating. No relationship were found between social media variables and disordered eating behaviors.
column83: The main limitation of this study was the sample size of the participants. Although measures were exhausted in the recruitmalet of participants, it may have been beneficial to have sent the recruitmalet materials out earlier in the off season as opposed to a month before the college gymnastics season started. Another limitation was the limited reliability data for the Social Hassles Questionnaire, as it is relatively new instrument and has not been extensively tested. Furthermore this study did not account for mental health status beyond possible disordered eating behaviors.
column84:
Since depression and anxiety have been linked to disordered eating patterns, future studies should also consider these pathologies, along with self-esteem. Research should aim to better understand the relationship between social media criticism and disordered eating behaviors in athletic populations. Athletes from different sports may respond differently to criticism than gymnasts, so it could be valuable to study these variables in other aesthetic sports, such as figure skating, diving, cheerleading, or even non-aesthetic sports like softball or basketball. Additionally, exploring these factors in males involved in aesthetic sports and the overall impact of social media on athletes' mental health could provide important insights.

It would also be beneficial for athletes, parents, and other significant figures in athletes' lives to be trained in recognizing the signs of disordered eating behaviors. Such training could help raise awareness of the potential dangers of social media platforms like Snapchat and offer guidance on how to support athletes if disordered eating behaviors arise.

To counter the effects of social media criticism on athletes, education initiatives should target coaches, families, friends, and athletes themselves to prevent the development of harmful eating behaviors and patterns, both now and in the future.

Another limitation was the limited reliability data for the Social Hassles Questionnaire, as it is relatively new instrument and has not been extensively tested. Furthermore this study did not account for mental health status beyond possible disordered eating behaviors.
column84:
Since depression and anxiety have been linked to disordered eating patterns, future studies should also consider these pathologies, along with self-esteem. Research should aim to better understand the relationship between social media criticism and disordered eating behaviors in athletic populations. Athletes from different sports may respond differently to criticism than gymnasts, so it could be valuable to study these variables in other aesthetic sports, such as figure skating, diving, cheerleading, or even non-aesthetic sports like softball or basketball. Additionally, exploring these factors in males involved in aesthetic sports and the overall impact of social media on athletes' mental health could provide important insights.

It would also be beneficial for athletes, parents, and other significant figures in athletes' lives to be trained in recognizing the signs of disordered eating behaviors. Such training could help raise awareness of the potential dangers of social media platforms like Snapchat and offer guidance on how to support athletes if disordered eating behaviors arise.

To counter the effects of social media criticism on athletes, education initiatives should target coaches, families, friends, and athletes themselves to prevent the development of harmful eating behaviors and patterns, both now and in the future.

column52: Motivations and Goals for Exercise-Related Behaviors
column82: Many of the psychosocial and socioemotional risk factors for disordered eating in the general population are also present in the undergraduate athlete population. Risk factors between male and Female differ in terms of presentation, but not necessarily on severity.
column83: The present study was cross-sectional, and data were self reported from a self-selected and predominantly Caucasian sample at one undergraduate university, which limits conclusion about causality and generalizability. The EDI-3 was developed primarily with Female, which may not capture eating behavior and body shape concerns of athletes of all genders. Although many of the included instruments used in the present study have been used amply within collegiate athletes samples, only the EDI has been independently validated for this population. We did not inquire or determine eating disorder diagnosis as we were interested in disordered eating risk more generally. Finally, because we were interested in the influence of team dynamics, our classification of non-athletes included those who engaged in personal exercise but not organized exercise, which may also convey similar eating disorder risk to those involved in organized sports. Given to observed differences between athletes and non-athletes, we do not believe that engagement in personal fitness influenced the results of this study.
column84: The cross-sectional nature of this study precludes a conclusion about causality. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify this relation. Given a comparatively higher focus on restrictive eating in athletes, more work is needed to confirm and better understand why Female athletes may engage in binge eating. Future reseachers should consider including the RMET as a behavioral measure of recognizing emotional expression in others that may measure different components of emotion regulation than self-report. Future researchers would do well to collect data from multiple campuses.

column5: Boyda, D., & Shevlin, M.

column30: Bodybuilding
column82: Anxiety was significantly associated with muscle dysmorphia. Anxiety and depression do not both mediate the relationship between victimisation experiences and muscle dysmorphia, the unique mediating effect of anxiety represents a possible and plausible route from childhood victimisation to muscle dysmorphia. Victimisation during childhood increases anxiety levels, as a consequence, individuals negatively evaluate their self-image resulting in a body image distorsion and ultimately muscle dysmorphia. Children who are victimised by family or peers during childhood via physical, verbal or social means may have an increased risk of developing a pathological fixation with their body and this may have an impact or increase the risk for muscle dysmorphia later in adulthood.
column83: The study was retrospective and cross-sectional and this as such limited conclusions regarding mediation. The study did not ascertain the temporal ordering of experiences which may limit analysis and interpretation, while childhood memories recalled during adulthood maybe subject to negative recall bias. In addition, it should not be discounted that the mediation model contained too few mediators to accurately predict an association between the childhood victimisation and muscle dysmorphia. Also the sample size was relatively small and this sample is not likely to be representative of the general population due to the sampling method. However, recruited participants through bodybuidling forum ensured adequate levels of variability in muscle dysmorphia scores: a general population sample likely have produced scores heavily positively skewed. Finally, low participation from the three large forums was unexpected.
column84:
A more appropriate recruitmalet strategy should be considered as an increased sample size xould contribute to more stable estimation of the mediation model. 
The future direction for a follow-up study should consider if such early experiences and subsequent manifestation of muscle dysmorphia lead to a gateway for the use of performance-enhancing drugs wich may further magnify the effects of msucle dysmorphia on their psychological functioning. This could be considered an important extension to this study as indivdiuals who use performance-enhancing drugs can rapidly change aspects of their muscularity including fat distribution as after all, this is the holy grail for those who have muscle dysmorphia.

column82: The study show that autonomous motivation for sport had a significant, indirect and positive association with drive for muscularity via perceived behavioral control and intention to gain muscle, and that contolled motivation for sports was related to drive for muscularity both directly and via attitude and intention to gain muscle mass. These results indicate that the trans contextual model was partially supported in the context of bodybuiling, suggesting a complex motivational model underlying drive for muscularity in male bodybuilders.
column83: Our data are limited because our sample was composed only of young male with different levels of expertise (i.e., non-competitors, future competitors, competitors), which might have influenced their motivation and engagement in drive for muscularity. Second, subjective norm is a questionable variable as it might indicate a measurement issue in the sense that such variables reflect greater pressure and controlling rather than supportive forms of motivation. Third, the date were collected using a self-report survey and might have been influenced by social desirability. Fourth, the internal consistency of some measures was quite low and this might have been linked to our heterogeneous sample or to the psychometric quality concerning the controlled motivation scale, or the inconsistency between the external regulation and the introjected regulation.
column84:
It would be interesting to conduct a longitudinal study to more closely examine the causal relationship between variables. Methodologically, an important perspective for the future would be to determine a cutoff for drive for muscularity, which might then function as a reference when using drive for muscularity as a screening instrument for disordered eating. Moreover, eating disorders are very common on male bodybuilders and it might be of value to examine the relationships between motivation for sport, drive for muscularity and other specified feeding or eating disorders such as food restriction or night eating syndrome, or binge eating. 
Preventive actions may be important for male bodybuilders, who focus on gaining muscle mass. Specifically, such actions should be directed toward helping them to avoid developing controlled motivation because, although motivation for sport of any kind can be a direct or indirect risk factor for the development of deviant behavior, controlled motivation seems to put them at greater risk. It may therefore be important to carefully keep track of the development of motivation for sport to be sure that controlled motivation stays low, with moderate and healthy practice of bodybuilding. Moreover, the motivational mechanisms explaining the development of drive for muscularity could be deepened by complementary analysis in terms of motivational profiles.

column83: First, our sample was composed of young male with different numbers of years of practice, hours of practice per week, and types of practices (i.e., noncompetitors, future competitors, competitors), which might infuenced their motivation and engagement. Second, the runners were older than the bodybuilders, and younger people are more at risk of developing eating disorders than older people. Third, the data were collected using a self-report survey and might have been influenced by social desirability. Fourth, no model/theory on body image in male was used, although body dissatisfaction was clearly present, and drive for muscularity was not considered. Fifth, our study was correlational. Sixth, it would be useful to determine a cutoff for eating disorders in male athletes because the EAT is not adapted to measure eating disorders in male athletes desiring to gain muscle mass. Finally, the motivational mechanisms explaining the development of eating disorders in male bodybuilders and runners who desire to gain muscle mass/lean body mass need to be further investigated in terms of motivational profiles.
column84:
Include the level of competition in the analyses. Another model that also takes into account sociocognitive variables, such as the Health Action Process Approach might be applied in future research. It would be interesting to conduct a longitudinal study to more closely examine causality in the relationships. An intraindividual approach would be more useful than an interindividual approach.

column84:
Its necessary and interesting for prevention to be carried out before the adolescent stage (before the age of 12 or 13). 
Implement health promotion programs where aspects of body image are also addressed in addition to working on eating and sport habits. Design interventions based on age, in addition to gender, since the data are increasingly similar between male and Female in terms of body image dissatisfaction and danger of ED. In the design of interventions, pay differentiated attention to the athlete and non-athlete population. Even within the group of athletes, it is recommaleded to differentiate according to modality for diagnosis, prevention and intervention. Finally, we would like to point out, two issues: First the young people participating in the study were not diagnosed, which shows that ecessive concern about physical appearance can lead to behavior or attitudes that affect health before the disease in diagnosed. Secondly, the results suggest the need for the development of longitudinal studies in which the variability of the different dimensions analized and their degree of influence on the risk of developing ED can be observed.

column82: Satisfaction of psychological need in sport was positively and significantly related to restrictive eating. The results revealed a full mediation effect of self-determination for sport in the association between frustration of psychological need in sport and restrictive eating behaviors. There is a significant negative association between self-determination for sport and restrictive eating behaviors in adolescent athletes. Being an elite athlete did not predict restrictive eating behaviors in our sample. Psychological needs frustration in sport more strongly predicts restrictive eating behaviors in girls, compared with boys. No significant moderation effect of gender was found in the association between satisfaction of psychological need and restrictive eating behaviors.
column83: First, the associations found between variables do not demonstrate any causal link because the cross-sectional design does not permit any inference about causality. This study used a large and diverse sample, it was not representative of all adolescents in the country, limiting the generalizability of the findings. In addition, problematic eating behaviors in this study refer to restrictive eating, measured by dietary restriction subscale of the EDE-Q. Therefore, the results cannot be extrapolated to other eating behavior problems, such as compulsive eating or binge eating. Moreover, since the instruments used to measure basic psychological needs in sport and self determination for sport were adapted slightly for the sport context by the research team, further studies should replicate these findings using other measures of these contructs. Lastly, constructs were tested with self-reported measures, and therefore, the results may have been influenced by social dsirability.
column84: Profesionals who guide young athletes in the regulation of their eating behaviors may benefit from more thorough consideration of self-determination and psychological needs specifically in the sport context. Moreover, both frustration and satisfaction of psychological needs in sports should be investigated because restrictive eating was associate with greater satisfaction of psychological needs in the present study. Thus, frustration of psychological needs in sport may be a better indicator of restrictive eating behaviors, especially in girls.

column82: There is a significant relationship between parental psychological control and both exercise dependence and eating disorder symptoms. Psychological control, both maternal and parternal, predicted maladaptive perfectionism, while maladaptive perfectionism, predicted ED symptoms and exercise dependence symptoms. Results confirmed the mediating role of maladaptive perfectionism as a full mediator for ED and exercise dependence symptoms for both male and Female habitual exercisers in the maternal data. In the paternal data, maladaptive perfectionism mediated the relationships between paternal psychological control and eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms as full mediator for the Female participants and as partial mediator for the male participants.
column83: First, the data were collected at one time point and not across multiple time points as it should be done for a true mediational analysis. Because of the cross-sectional and self-report design of our study, we cannot etablish either the direction or causality of the effects. As weel, the self-report data may have intrinsic limitations such as social desirability, so the use of objective and multi-informant measures and experimental designs are encourages. Although, our sample consisted of habitual exercisers, this sample was deemed justified, as eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms are prevalent in this population and because psychological control is a risk factor for eating disorder and exercise dependence symptoms in this population.
column84: The deleterious effects of parental psychological control, both on eating disorder and on exercise dependence symptoms, require the implementation of targeted interventions to educate parents in using fewer instrusions and parental autonomy support, as opposed to psychological control. It is important to educate parents about psychological control being a universally negative parenting strategy and to help parents identify and reduce the use of such dysfunctional practices. Parent training could be used to help parents to get to practice autonomy supportive skills by taking part in various exercices from common situations in familial daily living. Results of the study suggest that the therapist and client could work together to identify and correct the client's maladaptive perfectionism thought processes that result in maladaptive eating or exercise behavior.

column84: The deleterious effects of parental psychological control, both on eating disorder and on exercise dependence symptoms, require the implementation of targeted interventions to educate parents in using fewer instrusions and parental autonomy support, as opposed to psychological control. Coach and practicioners could incorporate aspects of emotional regulation interventions into practices or as supplemental activities to the season. For example, the coach could incorporate lunches with a sport psychologist, who could discuss emotional regulation tactics with the athletes. Similarly, the coach could incorporate goal-setting activities throughout the season, with a focus on how to set smart goals, and then how to regulate emotions through the challenges of achieving such goals.

column82: Ego orientation and performance climate were related to more frequent dieting, using more pathogenic weight control methods, greater perfectionism and perceiving more weight related peer pressure. Having a high ego orientation means that a Female aesthetic performer is sgnificantly more likely to report indices of disordered eating. Non-significant correlations were found between task orientation and DE. With respect to performance climate, significant relationships were found with all DE variables. The present study also shows that a mastery climate is negatively related to disordered eating. Mastery climate explained some of the variance of dieting frequency.
column83: A limitation in the present study was that we used a relatively crude measure for pathogenic weight control with limited reliability. Self-report holds the risk of both under or overstimation. Another constraint in the present study was the composition of our sample. column84: In future studes focusing exclusively on relationships between eating disorders or disordered eating with achievement motivation, full versions of general or sport specific measures could be administered such as the Eating Disorder Inventory-2 or the Female Athlete Screening Tool for disordered eating. Future studies should continue to making an effort to include objective measurements by the researchers or recent actual data provided by medical staff members. The observed relationships of this study should be replicated in future studies using larger samples of various athletes at risk for disordered eating. Roberts (2001) stated that a high ego orientation is particularly detrimental if it is accompanied by a low task orientation. Future research should further investigate if this is also true for disordered eating. To gain a more complete understanding of the relationship between ego orientation and disordered eating, future studies could also include the more recent 2 by 2 framework which not only distinguishes between ego and task orientation but also between approach and avoidance achievmalet goals. We therefore recommaled that coaches and teachers should create a mastery climate with its emphasis on personal development and interpersonal cooperation.

column82: The results showed that the athletic body image strongly contributed to eating disorder symptomatology. More specifically, the athletes self-evaluations about shape, weight and fat percentage and the perceived opinions of others on these aspects appeared to be only significant factors uniquely explaining 14 and 9% of the EDE-Q variance. On the other hand, although these athletic body image components were the only significant factors in the regression model, their contributions turned out to be rather limited. Moreover, thin-fat-self-evaluations in daily lifealso seemed to contribute to the equation although it did not reach significance. 64% of the variance was explained by the relevant body image components from daily life and sport.
column83: Limitations of the present study were its sample size and consitution. Unfortunately, the number of Dutch high performance athletes is not that extensive.
column84: Future studies should further explore athletes body comparisons in daliy life and sport, and possible differences between athletes with and without disordered eating in this respect. Future research should further explore body images in sport and daily life, particularly in athletes with disordered eating. We needed to extent the sample with a group of at-risk athletes who were not professionaly diagnosed in advance. Future investigation needs to take into account dynamic and contextual body image changes. It should also focus more closely on why certain athletes develop a more negative body image and how this could be prevented.

column14: The population was adults over the age of 18 years who participated in a diverse range of sport and exercise. The inclusion criteria of exercice twice or more per week was chosen to include people who exercised regularly but the criterion was relatively low as amount of exercise in not the defiing feature of compulsive exercise.
column30: Running, triathlon, ball sports (volleyball, football, baseball, basketball, golf, rugby, squash, netball, circket, hockey, tennis, badminton), gym, other (water polo, sailing, surf lifesaving, pilates, skateboarding, hula hooping, equestrian), cycling, dance, yoga, atheltics, rowing, swimming
column82: Direct and indirect effects were found between clinical perfectionism and eating pathology through compulsive exercise. Specifically, there were direct effects of clinical perfectionism on avoidance/rule driven behavior, weight control exercise, and mood improvement.
column83: Participant recruitmalet was not random or stratified which limits generalizability. The sample comprised mainly of individuals who are actively involved in one particular type of athletic poursuit: individual endurance sports and particularly running. The sample may, therefore, not be representative of individuals involved in sport and exercise in general. In addition, the study was cross-sectional, therefore the bidirectional relationship between eating pathology and compulsive exercise could not be assessed as this requires a longitudinal design. While we hypothesized that perfectionism would affect compulsive exercise, which would impact eating pathology, it could equally be argued that perfectionism influences eating pathology, which then influences compulsive exercise (i.e., compulsive exercise is a symptom of eating pathology, rather than an antecedent). Indeed, Meyer et al.’s (2011) model proposed bidirectional links between eating pathology and compulsive exercise. Meyer et al. (2011) argued that dieting and exercise reinforce one another due to social reinforcers which accompany the initial weight loss from regular exercise, which then intensifies eating, shape and weight concerns.
column84: It would be useful to determine whether interventions for both perfectionism and compulsive exercise may help to improve the efficacy of standard treatments for eating disorders, above the gain already found in efficacious treatments such as CBT-E (Fairbunr et al., 2009) where clinical perfectionism is a focus if it is elevated. Future research could also examine the efficacy of specific stand-alone treatments for perfectionism (e.g., Egan et al., 2014) for compulsive exercise and perfectionism in eating disorders. Future research should measure perfectionism, compulsive exercise and eating pathology at two time points using a panel design and include a cross-lagged effects to determine the bidirectional relations between variables.

column57: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
column82: Negative affect (depression and anxiety), and weight pressures in the dance environment were positively associated with ED symptoms. mental skills were found to be negatively asscoiated with ED symptoms. Negative affect partially mediated the relationship between weight pressures and ED symptoms. mental skills, specifically coping with adversity, freedom from worry, and confidence/achievement motivation, fully mediated the relationship between negative affect and ED symptoms. Total score for the athletic coping skill inventory was signficantly negatively correlated with weight pressure in dance, anxiety, depression and eating disorder risk.
column83: One limitation of this study was that the sample was predominantly white and Female. Results from this study may therefore not be generalizable to a more ethnically diverse sample or to male dancers. Furthermore, this study lacked a comparison group of non-dancers, which would have enabled the researchers to more objectively compare the impact of the dance environment with a non-dance environment.
column84: Additional studies are needed to explore how other protective factors (i.e., satisfaction with life, optimism, self-esteem, humor, and spirituality) may further explain variations in ED symptoms in dancers and contribute to this mediation model identified. Furthermore, including demographic variables in the analyses would help us to better understand if certain subpopulations of dancers, may be more at risk or protected from pressures in the dance environment. Finally, studies should include the use of alternative methods in addition to self-report to more thoroughly explore variables relating to the dance environment.

column14: The inclusion criteria were: having signed the informed consent form, training at least twho hours a day, five days a week, having participated in a regional competition in 2013, having answered the questionnaires, and having undergone anthropometric assessments. The exclusion criteria were: having physical and/or intellectual disabilities, and taking psychoactive medication periodically.

column55:
State Trait Anxiety Inventory-State (STAI-S)
State Trait Anxiety Inventory-Trait (STAI-T)
column82: The results of the first regression model (dieting) show that state and trait anxiety were not associated with long fasting periods in Female athletes. The regression model using the bulimia subscale score as the criterion variable showed that anxiety was not related to self-induced vomiting and binge eating in Female athletes. The last regression model showed that trait anxiety influences the type and amount of foods consumed by the athletes.
column83: One is the cross- sectional study design, preventing the inference of causality. This means that it is not possible to assess the intensity and direction of the associations found between the outcome variable and the independent variables. Another limitation may be the non-assessment of the athletes’ malestrual cycle phase since the malestrual cycle may affect anxiety.
column84: More specifically, coaches should pay attention to anxiety symptoms in their young athletes. Additionally, athletes’ anxiety level should be assessed by STAI. column84: Obligatory and non obligatory runners were dichotomized. It is likely, however, that this form of exercise occurs on a continuum and it would be valuable to assess this. Longitudinal research of those at risk form becoming obligatory runners could determine whether th shift towards obligatory running patterns occurs immediately after adopting an exercise regimen or whether the change occurs over time as they progress in training frequency, duration, and intensity. Further research using the Athletic Identity Measurement Scale in a variety of athletic population is necessary. Future studies should examine other mediating variables related to identity (motivation to exercise are variables associated with DE and obligatory exercise). It would be helpful to use the regulation in exercise questionnaire in conjunction with the obligatory exercise questionnaire and eating disorder measures to evaluate in more detail why certain individuals are more susceptible to unhealthy exercise attitudes and behaviours than others.

Coach and trainers should focus on athletic development programs that incorporate an exploratiion of athletes intrinsic values and help them connect their values to their poursuit of athletic goals. column82: A positive correlation was found between exercise dependence, orthorexic tendency and disordered eating attitudes. Higher EAT-40 scores were associated with lower ORTO-11 scores.
column83: Due to the cross sectional design, only associations bewteen exercise dependence and orthorexia and eating disorders could be determined, but it could not explain causality between the variables and whether exercise dependence is primary or secondary. The orthorexic tendencies of the students were evaluated with the ORTO scale. Studies reported that the psychometric quality of the ORTO scale was poor, as it was unable to distinguish between healthy and pathological healthy eating. The exercise dependence risks and eating behaviors of university students could not be examined according to exercise types due to the limited sample size.
column84: Future research should examine associations between these phenomalea according to exercise type in a larger sample. Healthy profesionals who work in the sports teams should be aware of these risks and monitor the students in terms of exercise dependence and orthorexia.

column55: 9-item subscale of the revised Eating Disorder Inventory
column82: Variables such as sex, age, BMI and body dissatisfaction explained 52% of the variance. Body dissatisfaction was the strongest predictor. Sports related variables were able to account for an additional 9% of variance in disorded eating. The most influential was the desire to be leaner to improve sports performance. General body dissatisfaction, sports-related body dissatisfaction was not a significant predictor for disordered eating. General and sports-related body dissatisfaction shared 37% of variance.
column83: Our sample size was too small to test for differences if gender was included in the analyzes as well. The EAT-26 was developed with non-athletic samples. The assessment of body dissatisfaction needs to be discussed critically. We opted for measures that focus on body fat and left out the dimension of muscularity. Nonetheless, muscularity might be important as to how athletes perceive their ideal body and more valid especially in male athletes. For ATHLETES questionnaires, limitations result from adapting and applying the questuonnaire within our sample.
column84:
Future studies could apply more differentiated assessments of disordered eating which allow analyzing if risk factors are the same for restricted and bulimic eating patterns. 
Achievement goal theory appears very promising for further studies that seek to understand the different risks for eating disorders in athletes. Longitudinal and experimental investigations are necessary to test whether the sports-related correlates of disordered eating tested in our study constitute risk factors for disordered eating and whether the assumed causal direction can be confirmed. A comparison between sport types regarding risk factors could help to explain why the risk for disordered eating is higher in certain sport types.

column82: Emotion dysregulation is an expected possible risk factor for both exercise addiction and eating disorders. column83: We adopted a cross sectional design and we conducted statistical mediation analyses. Although mediation might assume any casual relationships, our design and data are not suitable for confirming any cause and effect relationships. Furthermore, our model is based solely on theoretical assumptions and the current design cannot help to refute neither the alternative not the possible equivalent models. The nature of self rating instruments implies several possible biases (social desirability, insufficient self knowledge, distorsion of the memory processes) we should consider in interprating the results. The SCOFF questionnaire showed a questionable internal consistency in the present sample. We examined a wide range of regular exercisers which may down tune the exposed results, since in a group of high-volume exercisers the current findings may possibly be amplified.
column84: This study should be replicated with avid exercisers training for at least 10hr or more per week.

column83: Cross-sectional design, precluding examination of the directionality of the associations between SPA and DEAB. This study focused on the use of DEAB as a coping strategy for physical self-presentational concerns related to thinness or leanness. The fact that this study fails to consider concerns specifically related to muscularity and their possible relation with DEAB is an important limitation. We cannot identify the moderating role of the type of competition on the relationship between SPA and DEAB. column84:

One strategy that clinicians could adopt to prevent or reduce the development of high levels of DEAB in adolescents would be to focus on the reduction of high levels of physical self-presentation concerns , adopt healthy coping strategies for dealing with SPA levels.

column82: There is a significant and positive relationship between body related sport and exercise motives and generic DEAB and vomiting purging behaviors. The relationship between body related motives and DEAB may be amplified when adolescents practice individual and competitive sports and exercises. Involvement in sport and exercise for body related motives predicted higher levels of vomiting purging behaviours in adolescents involved in individual sports or exercises and do not generalize to those not involved in this type of practice. Involvement in sport and exercise for body related motives predicts higher levels of vomiting purging behaviours in adolescents who compete, but not in those who do not compete.
column83: The adolescents reporting exercising or practicing sports for at least one body related motive were coded in the category of body related motive. However for those indicating two or three motives, no information on the ranking of their motives was available. It is probable that adolescents for whom body related motives are only a minor reason for engaging in sport and exercise were still included in this category. This study relied on a cross sectional design, precluding examination of the direction of the associations between body related sport and exercise motives and DEAB. Only a small proportion reported exercising and practicing sports for a body related motive. This study neglected to examine more pathogenic behaviours (i.e., dieting, vomiting, fasting, use of laxatives and/or diuretics, enemas, appetite suppressants)
column84:
The relationship between body related sport and exercise motives and DEAB could be moderated by the physical self perceptions (e.g., physical condition, sport competence, flexbility). This hypothesis should be the object of future research. Little is known about the beliefs of youth with body related motives regarding sport and exercises as a means to attain their goal and their reasons for engaging in DEAB. These issues should be addressed in future research, particularly in qualitative studies. It would be interesting to focus more on the role of self presentation concerns (i.e., social physique anxiety) or socio-contextual factors (parents, peers, coaches) in the relationships between body related sport and exercise motives and DEAB. 
Preventive intervention should aim to encourage adolescents to become involved in sport and exercise for self-determined motives (e.g., social engagement and enjoyment) rather than for external motives (e.g., body related).

column5: Nieuwoudt, J.E., Zhou, S., Coutts, R.A., & Booker, R.
column7: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
column14: Adult males at least 18 years of age, individuals who are working out with weights (i.e., free weight or machines) at least 3 times per week and currently residing in Australia
column30: Weightlifting
column34: At least 3 days or more per week
column82: Significant correlation were found between muscle dysmorphia and body dysmorphic disorder symptoms. The correlational data suggested a relationship between the symptoms of muscle dysmorphia and eating disorders. Small but significant correlations were found between the substance use subscale of the MASS and the laxatives, diuretics behavioral question of the EAT-26, between the injury risk subscale of the MASS and the vomit and exercise behavioral questions of the EAT-26, and between the muscle satisfaction subscale and the binge eating and the lost > 9kg behavioral questions of the EAT-26.
column83: The EAT-26 may not be sensitive to muscularity oriented disordered eating and body image concerns. The current research consisted of an online survey, therefore the possibility existed that participants might have interpreted the meanings of questions or statements differently to those intended or might have perceived some of the statements or questions as vague. Self selection bias is a limitation of internet surveys. The data were exclusively based on self report which can have tendencies toward social desirability bias.
column84: A better understanding and awareness of the rates and symptoms of muscle dysmorphia and body dismorphic disorder and eating disorders may help strength and conditioning professionals to identify and refer at risk individuals for help from mental health professionals.

column83: The EAT-26 may not be sensitive to muscularity oriented disordered eating and body image concerns. Self selection bias is a limitation of internet surveys. The data were exclusively based on self report which can have tendencies toward social desirability bias.
column84: A better understanding and awareness of the rates and symptoms of muscle dysmorphia and body dismorphic disorder and eating disorders may help strength and conditioning professionals to identify and refer at risk individuals for help from mental health professionals.

column82: Body image related cognitive fusion was strongly associated with ED. A strong relationship was found between image related perfectionist self presentation and higher levels of disordered eating. Path analysis results demonstraed that the proposed model presents an excellent fit to the empirical data, accounting for 71% of the variance of disordered eating attitudes and behaviours.
column83: Cross sectional study limits any causal inferences. This study only focused on Female participants. Use of data exclusively based on self report measures. Considering that disordered eating is a multi determined phenomaleon, other emotional processes should be considered to explain this phenomaleon.
column84:
Future prospective studies should be conducted to clarify the associations between these variables and propose causal inferences. Also future research is needed to compare the acceptability and impact of cognitive behavioural therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy based interventions to promote athletes adaptive ways to deal with their body image. 
Data highlights the relevance of education programmes that promote more adaptive emotional strategies focusing on body image, to increase athletes defusion skills and the acceptance of unpleasant thoughts and emotions related to their body image. Our data seems to indicate that intervention and prevention programs for aesthetic athletes, should focus on the development of more adpative strategies related to body image, through the cultivation of a balanced and acceptance relationship with one's own body characteristics rather than on the adoption of body image related perfectionist self presentation strategies.

column84: Researchers should use measures of specific mood states (e.g., depression, anxiety) that are based on multiple items (e.g., PANAS-X), include measures of positive mood state (e.g., optimism, happiness, confidence) and incorporate designs (e.g., longitudinal) that allow these questions to be addressed directly. Professionals should be attuned to looking for subclinical level presentations of symptoms among the athletes with whom they work. Professionals may want to work proactively with male athletic teams, educating them about healthy, nutritional eating and maintaing regular exercise during the off-season. Such approaches may assist male collegiate athletes during the shift from the structural regimen that occurs when in-season and the potentially more relaxed, self-initiated approach that is taken during the off season.

column82: Perfectionism and body satisfaction explain dieting among Female athletes. For the male athletes, none of the predictors contributed to the understanding of their dieting behaviour. In addition, age, sport type and duration of sport participation did not contribute to dieting behaviour un case of male and Female. Adaptive and maladaptive perfectionism were associated with body satisfaction among Female athletes but not with dieting behaviour directly. Satisfaction with one's body was shown to be the largest independent predictor of dieting and their relationship was negative.
column83: The data was based on self reported measures. Cross sectional design limits the causal inference between perfectionism, body satisfaction and dieting. The sample consisted of athletes who were enrolled in a university program which might limit the generalizability. PANPS should not be used as a measure of perfectionism due to a questionable factor validity of the positive perfectionism subscale. EAT-26 was shown to have a low positive predictive value due to the rarity of targeted conditions while two out of three EAT-26 subscales demonstrated low internal consistency and omitting them while investigating eating disorder may not be the best approach. The number of Female participants was lower than males, which might have affected some of the analysis were gender-split was included.
column84: It would be important to further etablish the relationship between perfectionism dimensions and body satisfaction in the area of disordered eating but also take a consideration the context in which athletes perceive their body.

column82: Performance approach goals were positive predictors of emerging disordered eating attitudes. Mastery avoidance goals were also positive predictors of disordered eating attitudes. Performance avoidance was a protective factor. A relationship between mastery approach and disturbed eating attitudes did not emerge in the structural equation model or the correlation table.
column83: The data were self reported, suggesting the likelihood that social desirability was operative. The study was cross sectional, conclusions about causality cannot be inferred. The athletes scores on the eating psychopathology measure indicated relatively healthy attitudes, it is unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to athletes with more severe eating disorders. The generalization of the results is limited to the Female gender and an elite level. The participants ages and competition experience were not controlled.
column84:
Future studies might investigate whether the relationships can be generalized to athletes in other types of sport or to other types of population, as well as the aforementioned variables that could play a moderation or mediation role in this relationship. Future studies could replicate with a sample of non-athletic controls, as well as a clinical sample in order to determine whether the mechanisms involved in the eating psychopathology of athletes are also operative in the general population and patients with eating disorders. The contextual and temporal dimensions could be considered, with future studies examining the current eating behavior, with a temporal control especially concerning the current goals. 
Programs could be adapted to encourage an orientation toward task mastery as a means to protect from disordered eating attitudes.

column4: Scoffier, S., Paquet, Y., & d'Arripe-Longueville, F. (2010). Effect of locus of control on disordered eating in athletes: The mediational role of self-regulation of eating attitudes. Eating Behaviors, 11(3), 164-169. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eatbeh.2010.02.002
column5: Scoffier-Mériaux, S., Paquet, Y., & d'Arripe-Longueville, F.
column14: University students who regularly (i.e., 6h per week) practised a sport in regional and national competitions
column30: Soccer, volleyball, gymnastics and swimming
column55: Multidimensional Health Locus of Control Scale (MHLCS)
column82: We observed a negative influence of the locus of control attributed to the coach on the self regulation of eating attitudes in contexts of negative affect, social interaction and lack of anticipation of consequences on performance. The coach and sports firends contribute to maladaptive patterns of accomplishment and function as negative predictors of the self regulation of eating attitudes in several contexts. The results showed the positive influence of an internal locus of control on the self regulation of eating attitudes in the context of social interaction. We observed a negative influence of self regulatory eating attitudes on disordered eating in contexts of negative affect, social interaction and the absence of anticipation of consequences on performance. This study demonstrated the influence of an internal locus of control on disordered eating as mediated by self regulatory eating attitudes in a context of social interaction and the influence of an external locus of control, attributed to the coach and sports friends on disordered eating as mediated by self regulatory eating attitudes in context of negative affect, social interaction and an absence of anticipation of consequences on performance. This study did not reveal a significant influence of a locus of control attributed to the family or luck on the self regulation of eating attitudes in contexts of temptation or negative affect. The self regulation subscales were not significant in the contexts of food temptation and a lack of compensatory strategies.
column83: The data were self reported, which suggests that social desirability may have been a bias. The study used correlational and cross sectional methods, which limits the generalization of the relationships.
column84:
The social environment has a powerful impact on the development of disordered eating in athletes, the influence of these social relationship on athletes self regulatory eating attitudes merits further study, through an emphasis on locus of control and/or relationship quality. A longitudinal study would determine the stability of this impact and an experimental study would help to etablish the direction of the causality. 
The use of locus of control and self regulatory eating attitudes as concurrent variables may be useful to sports psychology practitioners in their work with athletes. They might also be used to evaluate an athlete ability to engage in new and better adapted eating strategies and to determine whether the development of new eating attitudes would benefit performance outcomes.

column82: After accounting for indices of psychological wellbeing (self esteem, anxiety and depression), having supportive teammate frienships was the best predictor of lower eating psychopathology. Modelling of teammates disordered eating behaviours and perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape were the best predictors of higher disordered eating . Perceiving pressure from teammates to lose weight/change shape, in addition to perceiving that teammates engaged in disordered eating attitudes and behaviours were the strongest mechanisms of influence associated with elevated disordered eating and exercise behaviours. For Females, eating and exercise psychopathology were more strongly associated with indices of negative teammate influences than for males.

column84: Future research should investigate whether susceptibility to teammate influences changes as a function of sport type and competitive level given research finding the athletes sport to be a key moderator in the development of disordered eating. Future research exclusively sampling athletes competing in team-based sports may indicate influences from teammates to have a greater impact on eating pathology.

column82: High level of anxiety mediated the relationships between teammates bulimic type behaviours and athlete engagement with drive for thinness behaviours and compulsive exercise to prevent negative affect and to control weight. Higher level of anxiety and depression were found to mediate the direct relationships between perceived pressure from teammates to lose weight or change shape and greater reported body dissatisfaction. column83: Although age and BMI were controlled for, it is acknowledged that there are a number of additional co-variates (e.g., perfectionism, athletic identity) that could have contributed to the findings of this study. The self report nature of the data collected and the context it was collected in (i.e., before/after a training session and in the company of teammates/coach) may potentially misrepresent athletes true behaviours. Items comprising the EDI-drive for thinness and body dissatsifaction subscales may not be an accurate reflection of male athletes experiences with disordered eating.
column84: Identifying key risk factors and relevant moderators and mediators for eating psychopathology is important for effectively identifying those athletes at increased risk of eating and exercise psychopathology, and for developing appropriately tailored intervention and prevention strategies. Future research into the role of teammates would benefit from experimentally manipulating mechanisms of teammate influence on athletes actual food intake and should consider employing methodologies that are specifically tailored to male athletes. Employing modeeling analytic techniques to further our understanding of the complex, multi-factorial influences on athlete eating and exercise behaviours.

column82: Critical comment severity was found to be more important than implicit teammate influeces when explaining increased drive for thinness, body dissatisfaction for Female athletes. Implicit teammate influences (i.e., bulimia modelling and teammate pressure) also have an increased role to play in disordered eating among Female athletes, it is noteworthy that this is not the case for male athletes where the severity of the critical comment was the only predictor of increased exercise psychopathology and drive for thinness.
column83: The critical comment group had a higher prevalence of athletes with an eating disorder history. It is possible that the critical comment was antecedent to their eating disorder. Cross sectional design, effect relationships cannot be determined. The social Hassless Questionnaire asks athletes to reflect on the impact of a single, albeit, harmful, critical comment. It is therefore not possible to ascertain whether the impact on wellbeing was from this particular comment or perhaps more likely from frequent comments received over time. The self report restrospective nature of the SHQ meant that the accuracy of findings could be limited by poor recall/reconstruction (e.g., some athletes referred to comments made several years ago).
column84:
Athletes and coaches could be mandated by their organisation to attend workshops highlighting how to combat negative body commentary (e.g., list of justifications for what is/is not appropriate communication) as well as equipping athletes with strategies to reduce body ideal internalisation (e.g., via media literacy training, enhancement of self compassion, promotion of body image flexibility). 
Future research should employ longitudinal designs with frequent sampling points which track athletes’ wellbeing in response to critical comments they receive from a variety of sources over time. Furthermore, future longitudinal research would benefit from exploring the impact of variables that may potentially mediate the relationship between critical comment severity and eating psychopathology. For example, poor psychological wellbeing has been found to exacerbate the relationship between negative teammate influences and eating outcomes, while self-compassion has been found to protect against the internalisation of weight stigma and social support seeking is a common coping strategy employed to reduce the negative impact of weight-related teasing. Finally, to improve specificity to male athlete populations, researchers should employ measures that assess muscularity enhancing behaviours that are also likely to be driven by critical comments.

column82: Avoidant attachmalet was associated with poor quality relationships with their influential parent and principal coach. Athletes who experiencd more conflict in their relationships were more likely to criticize themselves, which in turn can be related to low self esteem, with athletes feeling unvalued and worthless as indivdiuals. Subsequently, low self esteem was linked to higher depressive symptoms, which in turn was lined to eating psychopathology. Self critical perfectionism may play a more pivotal role in eating psychopathology than personal standard perfectionism. The possession of high self imposed standards may not be related to eating psychopathology. The psychopathological process of perfectionism and self esteem both seem to exert an indirect effect on eating psychopathology, while depression exerts a direct effect.
column83: The study was cross sectional. There are some limitations related to the operational definitions and measurement of the constructs related to the transdiagnostic cognitive behavioral model. In this study only one aspect of the concept of mood intolerance was captured. The current study employed self report measures, results are subject to social desirability and acquiescence response bias. The study did not use a control group of non athletes and a sample of athletes with eating disorders. It therefore remains unclear whether the relationships observed would extend to the nonathletic population or to clinical populations.
column84: Continuing to develop a more encompassing understanding of the risk factors associated with eating disorders in athletes (e.g., examining psycho-social risk factors in addition to the sport-specific risk factors) wa may come a step closer in being able to prevent, manage and treat the disorder within the broader sporting community.

column82: Societal pressures in the forms of pressures, information, and social media significantly predicted bulimic symptomatology a year later, mediated by general internalization.
column83: Poor reliabilities of measurement tools across time. Confirmatory factor analyses revealed issues with metric and scalar invariance, that while not so ill-fitting that structural equation modelling was invalid, this does show that gold standard measures from non-athlete studies do not perform as well within this athlete sample. Recruitmalet was done via social media and participants were rewarded with a voucher. These decisions may have encouraged careless or dishonest responding and meant some items and participants had to be removed from analysis. Increasing the number of time points either within the year period, or extending the research for a longer period would have allowed for even more sophisticated latent growth curve analysis, as ideally four or more time points are needed for nonlinear analysis.
column84: Future research should focus efforts on developing valid and reliable questionnaires to operationalise disordered eating, eating disorders, and related concepts specifically for athletes. How we operationalise, measure and therefore diagnose disordered eating and eating disorders in athletes needs to be tailored to them specifically. There is a power in words, and the wording must be appropriate to the context.

Future research should incorporate longitudinal designs to identify true risk factors of ED symptomatology and use qualitative interviews to further examine the lived experience of sport-related weight pressures. 
Practitioners may collaborate with other professionals, such as sports dieteticians, to educate skating communities on weight-performance myths and improve communication between skaters, parents, and coaches about the body. Practitioners may also assist athletes in coping with weight pressures by focusing on body appreciation and function while reinforcing that healthy training approaches can have positive effects on eating, exercise, and body image.

column82: Only the personality traits conscientiousness, emotional stability and agreeableness are significantly associated with disordered eating. Our mediation analyses revealed the relationship between conscientiousness and disordered eating was completely mediated via the path of exercise dependence and obsessive compulsive symptoms, while the relationship of emotional stability and disordered eating was partly mediated via exercise dependence symptoms and obsessive compulsive symptoms. Moreover the relationship between agreeableness and disordered eating was only mediated by the severity of obsessive compulsive symptoms. The results of the correaltion analysis revealed that conscientiousness, emotional stability and agreeableness were negatively associated with the severity of disordered eating. In contrast, extroversion and openness to experience did not show a significant association with ED. The multiple mediation model of conscientiousness on disordered eating revaled an indirect effect of conscientiousness on disordered eating via higher exercise dependence symptoms and higher obsessive compulsive symptoms. The multiple mediation model of the effects of emotiona stability on disordered eating demonstrated an indirect effect of emotional stability via exercise dependence and obsessive compulsive symptoms. Considering the single mediation model of agreeableness on disordered eating, our results showed that the relationship between agreeableness and disordered eating can be explained through obsessive compulsive symptoms.

column82: Wearing a uniform that emphasizes body concerns predicted increases in weight/shape concern during the 4-month observation period. Wearing a uniform that emphasizes body concerns did not predict increases in restrained eating behaviors. Perceived pressure for thinness from coaches predicted an increase in both weight/shape concern and restrained eating behaviors at time 2. Teammate pressure for thinness was solely predictive of restrained eating behaviors at time 2. Coach pressure for thinness was the only athlete-specific risk factor that was predictive of increases in both weight/shape concerns and restrained eating behaviors.
column83: The study time frame was relatively short, which may have limited the ability to detect change in weight/shape concern and restrained eating behaviors. Our sample had substantial attrition, with only about 54% of participants who completed time 1 completed the follow-up survey. The director of athletics and associated staff were present for the data collection , some athletes may have been concerned that the athletics department would have access to their data. There was a limited number of club athlete participants in the final sample, level of sport competitive could not be considered. There may be differences in competition level between club sport versus division I athletes. There are a number of measurement considerations.
column84:

column30: Basketball, cross-country, diving, gymnastics, lacrosse, soccer, swimming and track and field
column57: Social and Sport pressure related to significant others
column82: Weight pressures from parents, peers and the media were directly associated with body dissatisfaction, moreover these pressures were indirectly associated with disordered eating via their associations with thin and muscular ideal internalization. In the full model, weight pressures specific to the sport context were not associated with body dissatisfaction or disordered eating. The degree to which athletes internalized ideals for thinness and muscularity was associated with higher levels of disordered eating. Body dissatisfaction was not associated with disordered eating after other variables in the model were taken into account.
column83: A comprehensive understanding of sociocultural influences on disordered eating among athletes require not only greater representation of participants from marginazlied racial and ethnic groups, but also consideration of the role of intersecting marginalized identities (e.g., sexual orientation) and integration of qualitative and mixed methodological approaches that may more effectively characterizz the lived experiences of these athletes. Cross sectional design , it is not possible to determine whether these characteristics are risk factors for disordered eating or correlates of these behaviors.
column84:
There is a clear need for high-quality studies of athletes assessing weight related pressures, appearance ideal internalization, body satisfaction, and disordered eating over time. in addition to clarifying the temporal relationships among these characteristics, longitudinal designs could also address whether these relationships are stable at different stages of athletes careers or different time points throughout the athletic season. Future research sould also consider how sociocultural influences might contribute to positive eating-related outcomes, both in the sport context and more broadly. 
Interventions that specifically address the sociocultural pressures and appearance ideals most relevant to athletes, such as the Female Athlete Body Project, reduce risk for subsequent disordered eating behaviors. 
In addition to pressures and appearance ideals specific to the sports environment, eating disorder prevention programs for Female athletes should address general sociocultural pressures related to weight and appearance. These interventions should also address internalization of cultural ideals for appearance beyond thinness, for example dissonance-based interventions could challenge internalization of fit and muscular ideals and sport specific ideals for weight and shape. Interventions could also be enhanced by strengths-based approaches that build on elements of sport participation that appear to be protective, such as the contribution of athletes positive evaluations of their physical abilities and condition to body esteem.
